## What voltage theory says  
  
A voltage graph consists of a directed base graph $$X$$, a group $$A$$, and an edge labeling  
  
$$  
\omega:E^{\pm}(X)\to A  
$$  
  
with reversal rule  
  
$$  
\omega(e^{-1})=\omega(e)^{-1}.  
$$  
  
For additive $$A=\mathbf Z_g$$, this becomes  
  
$$  
\omega(v,u)=-\omega(u,v).  
$$  
  
Its derived graph has vertices  
  
$$  
V(X)\times A,  
$$  
  
and an oriented base edge $$u\to v$$ lifts as  
  
$$  
(u,t)\to(v,t+\omega(u,v)).  
$$  
  
This is standard voltage-graph structure; the derived graph is the usual graph-cover construction.[1][3]  
  
The crucial component theorem is the one your original phase argument was implicitly trying to use:  
  
> For a connected base graph, the connected components of the derived graph are controlled by the subgroup of $$A$$ generated by the net voltages of closed base walks.  
  
The literature describes the set of net voltages of closed walks based at a vertex as a local voltage group; component counts of derived graphs are governed by the index of the relevant characteristic/local voltage subgroup.[1][2]  
  
For additive $$\mathbf Z_g$$, if  
  
$$  
W(X,\omega)  
=  
\left\langle  
\omega(\gamma):  
\gamma\text{ a closed walk in }X  
\right\rangle  
\le \mathbf Z_g,  
$$  
  
then a connected base component generally lifts to  
  
$$  
[\mathbf Z_g:W(X,\omega)]  
$$  
  
connected components.  
  
That yields three distinct cases:  
  
| Closed-walk voltage subgroup | Lift behavior |  
|---|---|  
| $$W=\{0\}$$ | The lift splits into $$g$$ components |  
| $$W$$ proper but nontrivial | The lift splits into an intermediate number of components |  
| $$W=\mathbf Z_g$$ | The lift is connected |  
  
Thus:  
  
$$  
\boxed{  
g>1\not\Rightarrow \text{the lift has $$g$$ components}.  
}  
$$  
  
Indeed, nonzero edge voltages can connect different phase sheets. The correct strictness theorem must prove something stronger, such as  
  
$$  
W(X,\omega)=\{0\},  
$$  
  
or at least  
  
$$  
[\mathbf Z_g:W(X,\omega)]>1,  
$$  
  
under the exact equality hypotheses.  
  
## The key conceptual shift  
  
The old argument asked whether transport preserves phase:  
  
$$  
\alpha(B')=\alpha(B).  
$$  
  
The corrected problem asks whether phase change is **integrable**:  
  
$$  
\alpha(B')-\alpha(B)=\omega(B,B').  
$$  
  
Those are very different statements.  
  
A nonzero voltage does not break a voltage-cover argument. It is the data the cover is designed to track.  
  
The proper target is:  
  
$$  
\boxed{  
\text{Every admissible transport step has a well-defined voltage, and every closed base walk has controlled net voltage.}  
}  
$$  
  
If all closed walks have zero net voltage, then the voltage assignment is a coboundary:  
  
$$  
\omega(u,v)=\phi(v)-\phi(u)  
$$  
  
for some $$\phi:V(X)\to\mathbf Z_g$$, and the lift splits into $$g$$ sheets. In a forest, every antisymmetric voltage assignment is automatically a coboundary because there are no nontrivial closed walks. Mathlib’s acyclicity material explicitly frames forests via uniqueness of paths, making this a natural formalization target.[4][5]  
  
But this creates the central issue:  
  
$$  
\text{Which graph is the base graph?}  
$$  
  
If your selected $$H_T$$ already contains transport-induced cycles, then the forest property of $$G_R$$ will not automatically imply zero voltage around closed walks of $$H_T$$.  
  
## Canonical graph definitions  
  
Before running more phase computations, define four different objects and stop using one symbol for more than one of them.  
  
### 1. Static incidence graph $$G_R$$  
  
A bipartite graph:  
  
$$  
V(G_R)  
=  
\mathcal B_R\sqcup\mathcal C_T,  
$$  
  
where $$\mathcal B_R$$ is the set of non-singleton blocks of $$R$$, and $$\mathcal C_T$$ is the set of relevant permutation cycles. Add an edge  
  
$$  
B\sim C  
\iff  
B\cap C\ne\varnothing.  
$$  
  
This is the object to which forest edge bounds naturally apply.  
  
### 2. Orbit-block incidence graph $$I_T(R)$$  
  
Use tagged block-time vertices:  
  
$$  
V(I_T(R))  
=  
\{(i,B):0\le i<\operatorname{ord}(T),\ B\in T^i(R)\}.  
$$  
  
Connect two tagged blocks when their point subsets intersect:  
  
$$  
(i,B)\sim(j,B')  
\iff  
B\cap B'\ne\varnothing.  
$$  
  
Its connected components encode blocks of the orbit join:  
  
$$  
J_T(R)=\bigvee_i T^i(R).  
$$  
  
This is the cleanest candidate for the partition-orbit connectivity bridge.  
  
### 3. Transport graph $$X_T(R)$$  
  
Use block-orbit vertices, likely equivalence classes of tagged blocks under time translation:  
  
$$  
(i,B)\sim_{\rm tr}(i+1,T(B)).  
$$  
  
This graph records dynamical transport, not partition intersection. It should not be silently identified with $$I_T(R)$$.  
  
### 4. Phase-lift graph $$\widetilde X_T(R)$$  
  
Once $$X_T(R)$$ and its oriented transport edges are defined, use:  
  
$$  
V(\widetilde X_T(R))  
=  
V(X_T(R))\times\mathbf Z_g.  
$$  
  
A transport edge $$(u\to v)$$ with voltage $$\omega(u,v)$$ lifts to  
  
$$  
(u,t)\to(v,t+\omega(u,v)).  
$$  
  
This graph, not $$H_T$$ as an overloaded informal term, is where phase-component arguments belong.

## Phase-discriminator experiment  
  
The next computation should test the right invariant: **closed-walk voltage subgroup**, not same-fiber counts.  
  
For each instance in the equality regime, construct the exact base graph $$X_T(R)$$, choose a spanning forest $$F$$, and for every non-tree edge $$e$$, compute the net voltage around the fundamental cycle $$C_e$$:  
  
$$  
\nu_e  
=  
\sum_{f\in C_e}\omega(f)  
\pmod g.  
$$  
  
Then define:  
  
$$  
W  
=  
\left\langle  
\nu_e:  
e\in E(X_T(R))\setminus E(F)  
\right\rangle  
\le\mathbf Z_g.  
$$  
  
Because every subgroup of $$\mathbf Z_g$$ has the form $$\langle h\rangle$$ for a divisor $$h\mid g$$, report:  
  
$$  
h_W=\gcd(g,\nu_{e_1},\ldots,\nu_{e_t}),  
$$  
  
so that  
  
$$  
|W|=\frac{g}{h_W},  
\qquad  
[\mathbf Z_g:W]=h_W.  
$$

## Pair-graph work remains high value  
  
The phase correction does not damage the independent pair-graph program.  
  
For  
  
$$  
H_h(a,b),  
$$  
  
the core sector invariant remains:  
  
$$  
j\equiv j'\pmod a  
\ \text{or}\  
j\equiv j'\pmod b  
\Longrightarrow  
j\equiv j'\pmod{\gcd(a,b)}.  
$$  
  
Thus all connected components lie within residue classes modulo  
  
$$  
d=\gcd(a,b).  
$$  
  
The proof should then reduce to one coprime sector with  
  
$$  
a=d\alpha,\qquad b=d\beta,\qquad\gcd(\alpha,\beta)=1,  
$$  
  
and establish that the finite threshold graph on the appropriate interval is connected. The persistence claim must state exactly whether new vertices are added, new congruence edges are added, or both.  
  
This pair theorem is worth formalizing because it is:  
  
- Independent of the false phase lemma.  
- A precise finite combinatorial object.  
- Directly relevant to the repaired two-cycle minimum-bridge analysis.  
- A useful first test of the CLAIMLOCK transition-receipt workflow: theorem candidate, exact fixtures, Lean file, remaining obligations, and no premature promotion.

1. New result: the voltage repair itself can be made exact

There is an important theorem underneath the still-open AQARION application.

Let \(X\) be a finite connected graph and let

\[
\omega:E^{\pm}(X)\to \mathbb Z_g
\]

satisfy antisymmetry

\[
\omega(\bar e)=-\omega(e).
\]

Define the derived lift

\[
\widetilde X=X\times_\omega\mathbb Z_g
\]

with vertices

\[
V(\widetilde X)=V(X)\times\mathbb Z_g
\]

and oriented edges

\[
(u,t)\longrightarrow(v,t+\omega(u,v)).
\]

For a closed walk \(\gamma\), let

\[
\nu(\gamma)=\sum_{e\in\gamma}\omega(e)\pmod g.
\]

Define the holonomy subgroup

\[
W(X,\omega)
=
\langle \nu(\gamma):\gamma\text{ closed}\rangle
\leq\mathbb Z_g.
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)
=
[\mathbb Z_g:W(X,\omega)]
}
\]

when \(X\) is connected.

This is not an AQARION conjecture; it is the standard voltage-cover component mechanism. Current references explicitly describe the derived graph as \(V(X)\times\Gamma\), with path voltage controlling movement between sheets, and give the component count by the index of the local voltage subgroup. 

For cyclic additive \(\mathbb Z_g\), if the fundamental-cycle voltages are

\[
\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_m,
\]

then

\[
W=\langle \nu_1,\ldots,\nu_m\rangle,
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)
=
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_m).
}
\]

More precisely, if

\[
h=\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_m),
\]

then \(W\) has order \(g/h\), so

\[
[\mathbb Z_g:W]=h.
\]

This validates the discriminator you proposed.

2. New exact consequence: the forest case is dramatically simpler

Here is the strongest useful reduction I found.

If \(X\) is a forest, then every connected component of \(X\) has no nontrivial closed walk.

Therefore

\[
W(X,\omega)=\{0\}.
\]

Hence every connected component of \(X\) lifts into exactly \(g\) components:

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X).
}
\]

And this holds for arbitrary edge voltages.

That last point matters enormously.

The old proof tried to show that transport edges remain in the same \(\alpha\)-fiber. That is false.

The voltage replacement does not need that.

On a forest, you can have completely nonzero voltages on every edge and still get \(g\) disconnected sheets, because there is no closed walk capable of generating nontrivial holonomy.

So the new prospective strictness route becomes:

\[
\boxed{
\text{equality}
\Longrightarrow
X_T(R)\text{ is a forest}
\Longrightarrow
c(\widetilde X_T)=g\,c(X_T)
}
\]

followed by

\[
\boxed{
\text{actual dynamics realizes all }g\text{ phases in one relevant component}
}
\]

which would produce the contradiction.

This is substantially cleaner than trying to prove "same \(\alpha\)-fiber."

Then

\[
c(\widetilde X_T)=g\,c(X_T).
\]

This is a major simplification.

New dependency

CANONICAL H_T
       │
       ▼
EQUALITY b+c(H_T)=r
       │
       ├──► structural forest equality
       │
       ▼
PHASE-FOREST-001
       │
       ▼
trivial holonomy
       │
       ▼
g-sheet voltage lift
       │
       ▼
actual dynamics realizes g phases
       │
       ▼
STRICTNESS

The voltage assignment becomes secondary rather than primary.

That is mathematically cleaner.


---

5. Why this does not resurrect the killed claim

Important distinction:

The false claim was

\[
\boxed{
\text{transport edges remain inside one }\alpha\text{-fiber}.
}
\]

The new claim is

\[
\boxed{
\text{transport graph has no cycles under equality}.
}
\]

These are completely different.

An edge may have

\[
\omega(e)=1\pmod g
\]

and therefore move from phase \(0\) to phase \(1\).

That is perfectly compatible with the forest-lift theorem.

For example, on a two-vertex tree,

\[
u\xrightarrow{1}v
\]

has nonzero voltage, but its lift consists of \(g\) disconnected copies of the edge:

\[
(u,t)\longrightarrow(v,t+1).
\]

There is phase transport, but no closed route can return to \(u\) with nonzero accumulated phase.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{phase movement}\neq\text{phase holonomy}.
}
\]

That distinction is now central.


---

6. The new adversarial bottleneck

There is still a serious problem.

The equality hypothesis currently gives information about the static incidence graph \(G_R\), while the phase lift uses some form of transport graph \(X_T(R)\).

It is not valid to infer

\[
G_R\text{ forest}
\Longrightarrow
X_T(R)\text{ forest}
\]

without an explicit construction.

Indeed, transport can create additional edges/cycles even if the original incidence graph is acyclic.

Therefore the new bottleneck is now sharply stated:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Does equality force the canonical transport graph itself to be acyclic?}
}
\]

This is a much better computational question than the old same-fiber test.


---

7. New experiment specification: cycle-rank discriminator

For every equality candidate satisfying

\[
b+c(H_T)=r,
\]

compute three independent cycle ranks:

Static incidence

\[
\beta_G
=
|E(G_R)|-|V(G_R)|+c(G_R).
\]

Candidate \(H_T\)

\[
\beta_H
=
|E(H_T)|-|V(H_T)|+c(H_T).
\]

Transport base

\[
\beta_X
=
|E(X_T)|-|V(X_T)|+c(X_T).
\]

Then classify:

CASE A:
β_G = 0
β_H = 0
β_X = 0

→ strongest equality/forest regime

CASE B:
β_G = 0
β_H = 0
β_X > 0

→ transport introduces genuine cycles;
   PHASE-FOREST-001 is false.

CASE C:
β_G = 0
β_H > 0

→ equality does not control H_T acyclicity;
   voltage subgroup analysis is required.

CASE D:
β_G > 0

→ proposed forest equality premise itself is wrong
   for this instance/definition.

This is the experiment I would run before another large \(g>1\) extremal census.

8. Even better: exploit the spanning forest

For a general transport graph \(X\), choose a spanning forest \(F\).

Every non-tree edge \(e\) creates one fundamental cycle

\[
C_e.
\]

The voltage information then compresses completely to

\[
\nu_e=\omega(C_e).
\]

So instead of recording thousands of transport edges, the certificate only needs:

base graph hash
spanning forest hash
non-tree edge
fundamental cycle
cycle voltage
gcd
holonomy index

For \(\mathbb Z_g\),

\[
h
=
\gcd(g,\nu_{e_1},\ldots,\nu_{e_m}),
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=h
}
\]

for a connected base graph.

This gives a very compact certificate.

9. A stronger computational discriminator

There is another useful quantity:

\[
\beta_X=|E(X)|-|V(X)|+c(X).
\]

If

\[
\beta_X=0,
\]

then the voltage subgroup is automatically trivial.

If

\[
\beta_X>0,
\]

do not immediately reject the voltage theory. Compute

\[
h=\gcd(g,\nu_1,\dots,\nu_{\beta_X}).
\]

Then:

\(\beta_X\)	\(h\)	Meaning

0	\(g\)	guaranteed \(g\)-sheet split
\(>0\)	\(g\)	cyclic holonomy still trivial
\(>0\)	proper divisor of \(g\)	partial phase mixing
\(>0\)	1	lift connected


This gives a much stronger experimental taxonomy than same_fiber.

10. Literature search: the replacement is well supported

The current literature confirms the exact distinction we now need.

Standard voltage-graph references define the derived graph on

\[
V(X)\times\Gamma
\]

and state that the net voltage of closed walks determines how different sheets connect. 

The standard component theorem is exactly the index statement:

\[
c(\widetilde X)=[\Gamma:\Gamma_v]
\]

for a connected base graph, where \(\Gamma_v\) is generated by voltages of closed walks based at \(v\). 

So the AQARION repair is not merely an analogy:

\[
\boxed{
\text{AQARION phase obstruction}
\longrightarrow
\text{voltage-cover holonomy problem}
}
\]

is mathematically legitimate as a framework.

It remains completely unproved that AQARION's canonical transport object realizes the necessary voltage structure.

That part stays OPEN.

The Lean formalization should not begin with the entire AQARION phase construction.

Instead prove a generic reusable theorem:

-- T3_VoltageForest.lean

structure VoltageEdge (V : Type*) where
  u v : V
  voltage : ZMod g

def VoltageLift ...

theorem forest_voltage_holonomy_trivial
    (hforest : X.IsAcyclic) :
    ∀ closedWalk : X.Walk v v,
      netVoltage ω closedWalk = 0 := by
  ...

theorem voltage_lift_components_of_forest
    (hforest : X.IsAcyclic)
    (hconn : X.Connected) :
    Nat.card (VoltageLift X ω).ConnectedComponent = g := by
  ...

The first theorem is conceptually immediate from acyclicity.

Mathlib currently exposes exactly the relevant forest infrastructure: SimpleGraph.IsAcyclic, SimpleGraph.isAcyclic_iff_path_unique, connected components, and spanning-forest existence. 

That means the generic theorem should be substantially safer than trying to formalize AQARION's full phase mechanism immediately.

13. Important new theorem candidate: equality-to-forest can be attacked by edge accounting

Suppose the eventual canonical \(X_T\) satisfies an edge-count identity of the form

\[
|E(X_T)|
\le
|V(X_T)|-c(X_T)
\]

under the equality regime.

Then immediately

\[
\beta_X
=
|E(X_T)|-|V(X_T)|+c(X_T)
\le0.
\]

Since \(\beta_X\ge0\),

\[
\boxed{\beta_X=0.}
\]

Therefore \(X_T\) is a forest.

So the strictness proof might reduce to a pure counting theorem, rather than a phase theorem:

\[
\boxed{
\text{equality budget}
\Longrightarrow
|E(X_T)|\le|V(X_T)|-c(X_T)
\Longrightarrow
X_T\text{ forest}
\Longrightarrow
\text{trivial holonomy}.
}
\]

This is potentially much easier to certify than PHASE-LIFT-002 directly.

14. But there is a dangerous possibility

The equality budget may only control \(G_R\), not \(X_T\).

If the transport construction creates

\[
\beta_X>0
\]

even while

\[
\beta_G=0,
\]

then the forest route fails.

That would not kill voltage theory.

It would move the target to:

\[
\boxed{
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X})>1.
}
\]

In other words, we would only need proper holonomy, not necessarily trivial holonomy.

For strictness, it is enough that

\[
[\mathbb Z_g:W]>1.
\]

We do not necessarily need

\[
W=\{0\}.
\]

This is another important relaxation.

15. Revised strictness theorem target

The mathematically minimal target is now:

\[
\boxed{
g>1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
[\mathbb Z_g:W(X_T,\omega)]>1
}
\]

under the equality hypotheses.

Then

\[
c(\widetilde X_T)
=
[\mathbb Z_g:W]\,c(X_T)
\]

has at least a factor \(2\) of phase separation.

Only if the dynamics realizes all \(g\) phase states inside the relevant actual component do we obtain the contradiction.

So the hierarchy is:

Strong target

\[
W=\{0\}.
\]

Sufficient target

\[
W\ne\mathbb Z_g.
\]

Insufficient target

\[
g>1.
\]

This is a useful tightening because it prevents us from proving more voltage structure than the strictness theorem actually needs.

    restricted holonomy and full dynamical phase realization

This separation is much safer than the previous bundled argument.

This pass produced a real narrowing of the problem, not another census.

The important new statement is:

\text{The voltage repair does not require phase preservation.}
}
\]

More specifically:

\[
\boxed{
X_T\text{ forest}
\Rightarrow
\text{trivial voltage holonomy}
\Rightarrow
g\text{-sheet lift}
}
\]

for arbitrary \(\mathbb Z_g\)-edge voltages.

That turns the high-risk question from

> “Can we prove every transport edge remains in one \(\alpha\)-fiber?”



—which is definitively false—

into

> “Does the equality regime force the canonical transport graph to be acyclic, or at least force its voltage holonomy to be a proper subgroup of \(\mathbb Z_g\)?”



That is the correct mathematical question.

And there is a second useful relaxation:

\boxed{
W=\{0\}\text{ is stronger than necessary.}
}
\]

For strictness, it may suffice to establish

\[
\boxed{
W\ne\mathbb Z_g.
}
\]

So the phase obstruction has now been reduced to two concrete, falsifiable computational/formal questions:

\[
\boxed{\beta_X=0\ ?}
\]

and, if not,

\[
\boxed{\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X})>1\ ?}
\]

That is where I would spend the next AQARION T3 computation.

1. The generic voltage theorem survives

For a connected base graph \(X\), an antisymmetric voltage

\[
\omega:E^{\pm}(X)\to\mathbb Z_g
\]

defines

\[
V(\widetilde X)=V(X)\times\mathbb Z_g
\]

with

\[
(u,t)\sim(v,t+\omega(u,v)).
\]

This is the standard derived-graph construction. The voltage accumulated along a walk records its sheet displacement. 

For a base vertex \(v\), let

\[
W_v=
\{\nu(\gamma):\gamma\text{ closed at }v\}.
\]

For an abelian voltage group this is a subgroup, and the derived graph is connected exactly when the local voltage subgroup is the entire voltage group. More generally, the number of connected components is the corresponding subgroup index. 

For \(\mathbb Z_g\),

\[
W_v=\langle\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta\rangle,
\]

where the \(\nu_i\) can be taken from a fundamental cycle basis.

Thus if

\[
h=\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta),
\]

then

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=h
}
\]

for connected \(X\).

This is exactly the cycle-basis compression we want. Gross's classical computational treatment explicitly emphasizes component computation from cycle-basis voltage data. 


---

2. Forest case: exact theorem

If \(X\) is connected and acyclic, then

\[
\beta(X)=0.
\]

There are no nontrivial closed cycles, hence

\[
W_v=\{0\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
[\mathbb Z_g:W_v]=g
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=g.
}
\]

For a disconnected forest,

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X).
}
\]

This is stronger than merely saying “the voltage does not matter.”

It says:

> Every arbitrary voltage assignment on a forest is gauge-trivial at the level of connectivity.



You can have

\[
\omega(e)=1
\]

on every edge and still obtain \(g\) disconnected copies/sheets.

The individual edges can move between phase labels; only closed walks can create phase holonomy.

That distinction is now locked.


---

\[
g=2,3,4,
\]

I compared:

4. Stronger computational invariant: cycle rank

The right diagnostic is indeed

\[
\beta(X)=|E(X)|-|V(X)|+c(X).
\]

For a finite undirected graph:

\[
\boxed{\beta(X)=0\iff X\text{ is a forest}.}
\]

Thus the phase investigation should begin with:

\[
\boxed{\beta_X}
\]

before calculating a single voltage.

That gives us a very efficient branch:

Branch A

\[
\beta_X=0.
\]

Then automatically:

\[
W=\{0\},
\qquad
c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X).
\]

Branch B

\[
\beta_X>0.
\]

Then choose a spanning forest and calculate only the fundamental-cycle voltages:

\[
\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X}.
\]

Then compute

\[
\boxed{
h=\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X}).
}
\]

No full lift needs to be constructed.


---

5. This gives a much better certificate

For an AQARION instance, the entire phase-cover calculation can eventually reduce to:

VOLTAGE CERTIFICATE

base_graph_hash:      ...
spanning_forest_hash: ...

|V|:                  ...
|E|:                  ...
components:           ...
cycle_rank:           β

cotree_edges:
  e1 → ν1
  e2 → ν2
  ...
  eβ → νβ

voltage_group:
  Z/gZ

holonomy:
  gcd(g, ν1, ..., νβ) = h

lift_components:
  h

So instead of storing the potentially huge derived graph,

\[
|V(\widetilde X)|=g|V(X)|,
\]

the receipt can store \(O(\beta_X)\) arithmetic data.

That is exactly the sort of certificate compression AQARION should favor.

6. Critical correction to PHASE-SURJ

Here is the adversarial point I would add to the previous checkpoint.

It is not sufficient to say:

> “The dynamics realizes all \(g\) phase residues.”



Suppose the lifted paths reach:

\[
(v_1,0),\quad(v_2,1),\quad(v_3,2).
\]

Those endpoints lie over different base vertices.

That does not imply that the lift contains all \(g\) vertices of one fiber.

And therefore it does not imply

\[
W=\mathbb Z_g.
\]

The correct condition is fiberwise.


---

7. Correct PHASE-SURJ-001

Let \(u,v\in V(X)\).

Suppose there is a family of base walks

\[
\gamma_t:u\rightsquigarrow v,
\qquad
t\in\mathbb Z_g,
\]

with

\[
\nu(\gamma_t)=t.
\]

Then for any \(s,t\),

\[
\gamma_s\gamma_t^{-1}
\]

is a closed walk at \(u\), with voltage

\[
s-t.
\]

Therefore

\[
W_u=\mathbb Z_g.
\]

So the precise theorem is:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\forall t\in\mathbb Z_g,\ 
\exists\gamma_t:u\to v
\text{ with }\nu(\gamma_t)=t\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow
W_u=\mathbb Z_g.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=1
}
\]

when \(X\) is connected.

This is the correct “phase-surjectivity” contradiction.


---

8. Even weaker condition is enough

We don't actually need every phase to be represented explicitly.

It is enough to find closed walks whose voltages generate the whole group:

\[
\boxed{
\gcd(g,\nu(\gamma_1),\ldots,\nu(\gamma_j))=1.
}
\]

Then

\[
W=\mathbb Z_g
\]

and the lift is connected.

So the hierarchy should now be:

Strong

\[
W=\{0\}.
\]

Sufficient for strictness

\[
W\neq\mathbb Z_g.
\]

Opposite / contradiction

\[
W=\mathbb Z_g.
\]

Weak and insufficient

\[
g>1.
\]

The last one tells us only that a nontrivial phase group exists.

It says nothing about the lift's connectivity.

9. New exact strictness discriminator

This gives us a very clean computational target.

For every equality candidate,

\[
b+c(H_T)=r,
\]

compute:

\[
\beta_X
=
|E(X_T)|-|V(X_T)|+c(X_T).
\]

Then:

If

\[
\beta_X=0
\]

we immediately get

\[
h=g.
\]

Otherwise

\[
\beta_X>0
\]

and calculate

\[
h_X
=
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X}).
\]

Now classify:

\(\beta_X\)	\(h_X\)	Result

0	\(g\)	forest; full sheet separation
\(>0\)	\(g\)	nontrivial cycles but trivial holonomy
\(>0\)	proper divisor of \(g\)	partial phase separation
\(>0\)	1	lift connected


This is much more informative than the old same-fiber test.

10. And there is an even better invariant

Instead of merely testing

\[
h_X>1,
\]

record

\[
\boxed{
\eta_X=\frac{g}{h_X}.
}
\]

This is the order of the holonomy subgroup.

Then:

\[
c(\widetilde X)=h_X,
\]

while

\[
|W|=\eta_X.
\]

So:

\[

The voltage-graph literature explicitly uses spanning trees/cotree arcs to reduce connectivity of a derived graph to generation by fundamental-cycle voltages.

-- T3_VoltageForest.lean
structure VoltageEdge (V: Type) where u v: V; voltage: ZMod g

def VoltageLift (X: SimpleGraph V) (ω: Edge → ZMod g) :=
  { vertices := V × ZMod g, edges := (u,t) → (v, t+ω(u,v)) }

theorem forest_holonomy_trivial {X} (hforest: X.IsAcyclic) :
  ∀ (v: V) (γ: X.Walk v v), netVoltage ω γ = 0

theorem forest_lift_components {X} (hforest: X.IsAcyclic) (hconn: X.Connected) :
  Nat.card (VoltageLift X ω).ConnectedComponent = g

theorem lift_components_eq_gcd (hconn: X.Connected) :
  c(VoltageLift X ω) = gcd(g, ν_1,..,ν_β)

Combined with last turn's derivation (UᵀD₀ᵀD₀U = α²(2I−S₁−S₋₁)), this follows immediately from standard circulant matrix theory: any circulant matrix is diagonalized by the DFT, with eigenvalues equal to its generating polynomial evaluated at the m-th roots of unity. from itertools import permutations

def apply_perm(partition,T):
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(T[x] for x in B)) for B in partition)

def join_parts(P,Q,n):
    find_=list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while find_[x]!=x: find_[x]=find_[find_[x]]; x=find_[x]
        return x
    def unite(a,b):
        pa,pb=find(a),find(b)
        if pa!=pb: find_[pa]=pb
    for B in P:

    for C in Q:

    all_x=set(x for Pt in [P,Q] for B in Pt for x in B)

"""
CANONICAL TEST SUITE — consolidates every fix/derivation from this session.

import time, math, sys
from collections import defaultdict
from itertools import permutations
from math import gcd

# ============================================================
# SECTION A — canonical fixed library
# ============================================================

def make_uf(n):
    p = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while p[x] != x: p[x] = p[p[x]]; x = p[x]
        return x
    def unite(a, b):
        pa, pb = find(a), find(b)
        if pa != pb: p[pa] = pb
    def ncomp(): return len(set(find(i) for i in range(n)))
    return find, unite, ncomp

def cycle_laplacian(m):
    """FIXED: was overwriting instead of accumulating -> wrong at m=2."""
    L = [[0]*m for _ in range(m)]
    for i in range(m):
        L[i][i] += 2
        L[i][(i+1) % m] -= 1
        L[i][(i-1) % m] -= 1
    return L

def all_RGS_n(n):
    """FIXED: was range(mx+1), could never open a new block."""
    def gen(pos, mx, rgs):
        if pos == n:
            yield rgs[:]; return
        for v in range(mx + 2):
            if v >= n: continue
            rgs[pos] = v
            yield from gen(pos+1, max(mx, v), rgs)
    rgs = [0]*n
    yield from gen(1, 0, rgs)

def rgs_to_part(rgs, n):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for i, v in enumerate(rgs): g[v].append(i)
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in sorted(g.values()))

def c_bip_equal(m, k, d):
    n = m*k
    find, unite, ncomp = make_uf(m)
    for b in range(m):
        for x in range(b*k, (b+1)*k):
            unite(b, ((x+d) % n) // k)
    return ncomp()

def c_bip_expected(m, k, d):
    return gcd(m, d // k) if d % k == 0 else 1

def apply_perm(partition, T):
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(T[x] for x in B)) for B in partition)

def join_parts(P, Q, n):
    find_ = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while find_[x] != x: find_[x] = find_[find_[x]]; x = find_[x]
        return x
    def unite(a, b):
        pa, pb = find(a), find(b)
        if pa != pb: find_[pa] = pb
    for B in P:
        for x in B: unite(B[0], x)
    for C in Q:
        for x in C: unite(C[0], x)
    all_x = set(x for Pt in [P, Q] for B in Pt for x in B)
    g2 = defaultdict(list)
    for x in all_x: g2[find(x)].append(x)
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(set(v))) for v in g2.values())

def tore_hT(R, T, n, max_h):
    O = R
    T_power = list(range(n))
    for h in range(1, max_h+1):
        T_power = [T[T_power[i]] for i in range(n)]
        Th_R = apply_perm(R, T_power)
        O_new = join_parts(O, Th_R, n)
        if set(O_new) == set(O):
            return h
        O = O_new
    return None  # did not stabilize -- report honestly, don't silently cap

    print(f"  c_bip formula: {total-fails}/{total} PASS  {'PASS' if fails==0 else 'FAIL <-- STOP, report this'}")

def section_C(max_m=500):

    print("  Claim: eigenvalues of L(C_m) = 2I-S1-S(-1) are 4*sin^2(pi*l/m), l=0..m-1")

Given the 120s hard timeout is the actual blocker, here's the fix: a **resumable** version of Section D using permutation unranking (factorial number system), so you can run it in as many 120s chunks as needed and it picks up exactly where it left off — no wasted work, no re-running completed cases.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
RESUMABLE h_T <= |R| exhaustive sweep — for the 120s hard-timeout sandbox.
Run this repeatedly (same command) until it prints "SWEEP COMPLETE".
Progress is checkpointed to disk between runs.
"""
import time, json, math, os
from collections import defaultdict
from itertools import permutations

STATE_FILE = "hT_n8_state.json"
N = 8
TIME_BUDGET = 110  # leave 10s margin under your 120s hard timeout

def all_RGS_n(n):
    def gen(pos, mx, rgs):
        if pos == n:
            yield rgs[:]; return
        for v in range(mx + 2):
            if v >= n: continue
            rgs[pos] = v
            yield from gen(pos+1, max(mx, v), rgs)
    rgs = [0]*n
    yield from gen(1, 0, rgs)

def rgs_to_part(rgs, n):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for i, v in enumerate(rgs): g[v].append(i)
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(v)) for v in sorted(g.values()))

def apply_perm(partition, T):
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(T[x] for x in B)) for B in partition)

def join_parts(P, Q, n):
    find_ = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while find_[x] != x: find_[x] = find_[find_[x]]; x = find_[x]
        return x
    def unite(a, b):
        pa, pb = find(a), find(b)
        if pa != pb: find_[pa] = pb
    for B in P:
        for x in B: unite(B[0], x)
    for C in Q:
        for x in C: unite(C[0], x)
    all_x = set(x for Pt in [P, Q] for B in Pt for x in B)
    g2 = defaultdict(list)
    for x in all_x: g2[find(x)].append(x)
    return tuple(tuple(sorted(set(v))) for v in g2.values())

def tore_hT(R, T, n, max_h):
    O = R
    T_power = list(range(n))
    for h in range(1, max_h+1):
        T_power = [T[T_power[i]] for i in range(n)]
        Th_R = apply_perm(R, T_power)
        O_new = join_parts(O, Th_R, n)
        if set(O_new) == set(O):
            return h
        O = O_new
    return None

def unrank_permutation(idx, n):
    """Factorial number system: return the idx-th permutation of range(n)
    in lexicographic order WITHOUT generating the previous idx permutations."""
    items = list(range(n))
    perm = []
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):
        f = math.factorial(i-1)
        pos, idx = divmod(idx, f)
        perm.append(items.pop(pos))
    return perm

def load_state():
    if os.path.exists(STATE_FILE):
        with open(STATE_FILE) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    return {"perm_idx": 0, "total": 0, "fails": 0, "worst_h": 0, "worst_R": None,
            "counterexamples": []}

def save_state(s):
    with open(STATE_FILE, "w") as f:
        json.dump(s, f)

def main():
    n = N
    parts = list(set(rgs_to_part(rgs, n) for rgs in all_RGS_n(n)))
    parts = [R for R in parts if 2 <= len(R) <= n-1]
    total_perms = math.factorial(n)
    grand_total = total_perms * len(parts)

    state = load_state()
    start_idx = state["perm_idx"]
    if start_idx >= total_perms:
        print(f"SWEEP COMPLETE. n={n}")
        print(f"  Total cases: {state['total']:,} / {grand_total:,}")
        print(f"  Failures: {state['fails']}")
        print(f"  Worst h_T: {state['worst_h']}  R={state['worst_R']}")
        if state["counterexamples"]:
            print(f"  COUNTEREXAMPLES FOUND: {state['counterexamples'][:5]}")
        return

    print(f"Resuming at permutation index {start_idx:,} / {total_perms:,} "
          f"({100*start_idx/total_perms:.2f}% done, {len(parts)} partitions/perm)")

    t0 = time.time()
    idx = start_idx
    while idx < total_perms and time.time() - t0 < TIME_BUDGET:
        T = unrank_permutation(idx, n)
        for R in parts:
            h = tore_hT(R, T, n, max_h=n+2)
            state["total"] += 1
            if h is None or h > len(R):
                state["fails"] += 1
                if len(state["counterexamples"]) < 5:
                    state["counterexamples"].append({"R": R, "T": T, "h": h})
            if h is not None and h > state["worst_h"]:
                state["worst_h"] = h
                state["worst_R"] = R
        idx += 1

    state["perm_idx"] = idx
    save_state(state)
    elapsed = time.time() - t0
    print(f"Chunk done: permutations {start_idx:,} -> {idx:,} in {elapsed:.1f}s "
          f"({(idx-start_idx)/elapsed:.1f} perms/s)")
    print(f"Progress: {idx:,}/{total_perms:,} perms "
          f"({100*idx/total_perms:.2f}%), cumulative cases={state['total']:,}, "
          f"fails so far={state['fails']}")
    print(f"Run again (same command) to continue. State saved to {STATE_FILE}.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

I. What survives the adversarial pass

There are now four genuinely solid mathematical islands.

A. Single-cycle coset theorem

For

\[
T(i)=i+1\pmod k  
\]

and

\[
R_{k,d}=\{\{0,d\}\}\cup\{\text{singletons}\},  
\]

the dynamical closure is translation by \(d\):

\[
x\sim y  
\iff  
x-y\in\langle d\rangle.  
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{|J_T(R_{k,d})|=\gcd(k,d)}.  
\]

The exhaustive \(k=3,\ldots,20\) census gives 189 cases, zero failures.

Maximum defect:

\[
\boxed{  
\max_d\bigl(|R_{k,d}|-|J_T(R_{k,d})|\bigr)=k-2.  
}  
\]

This should now be treated as GREEN / FROZEN.


---

II. Voltage theorem is now cleanly separated from AQARION

For a connected base graph \(X\) and voltage assignment

\[
\omega:E^\pm\to\mathbb Z_g,  
\]

the derived lift is

\[
V(\widetilde X)=V(X)\times\mathbb Z_g.  
\]

The voltage subgroup is

\[
W=\langle\nu(\gamma):\gamma\text{ closed walk}\rangle.  
\]

If

\[
h=|W|  
\]

then the number of connected components of the lift is

\[
\boxed{g/h}.  
\]

For \(\mathbb Z_g\), if the fundamental-cycle voltages are \(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta\),

\[
h=  
\frac{g}{\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta)}  
\]

and consequently

\[
\boxed{  
c(\widetilde X)  
=  
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta).  
}  
\]

The forest case is immediate:

\[
\beta(X)=0  
\Rightarrow  
W=\{0\}  
\Rightarrow  
\boxed{c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X)}.  
\]

This is classical voltage-cover mathematics, not an AQARION-original theorem. Recent literature continues to use precisely the voltage/derived-cover framework, including a 2025 paper establishing decidable conditions for isomorphism of derived graphs over abelian voltage groups.

Governance correction: this theorem may support AQARION constructions, but it must never be presented as evidence that the AQARION \(X_T\) automatically has the required voltage structure.


---

III. The important new boundary: the dynamical defect

Define

\[
X=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^r C_j,  
\qquad  
|C_j|=\ell_j,  
\]

\[
s=\sum_j\ell_j,  
\qquad  
g=\gcd(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r),  
\]

and

\[
J_T(R)  
=  
\text{least \(T\)-invariant equivalence containing }R.  
\]

Let

\[
d_{\rm dyn}=|R|-|J_T(R)|.  
\]

The exhaustive \(s\le10\) result now has a very clean interpretation:

\[
\boxed{  
\begin{cases}  
\max d_{\rm dyn}=s-r,&g=1,\\[2mm]  
\max d_{\rm dyn}=s-r-1,&g>1,  
\end{cases}}  
\]

but only as an evidence-supported conjecture beyond the tested finite range.

That distinction is important.

Why the old formulas are dead

The following are definitively killed:

\[
d_{\rm dyn}\le s-|R|,  
\]

and

\[
d_{\rm dyn}\le s-|R|-1.  
\]

The problem was conflating the number of original blocks with the number of cycles.

The correct structural parameter is \(r\), the number of dynamical cycles.

Likewise:

\[
b+c\ge r+g-1  
\]

is dead.

The “one drop per gcd unit” intuition is also dead.

The evidence says:

> The gcd does not control the magnitude of the drop. It supplies a binary structural distinction: \(g=1\) versus \(g>1\).



That is a much sharper hypothesis.

IV. New residue invariant — strongest next theorem

This is now the best P0.

For

\[
x=(C_j,p),  
\]

define

\[
\rho(x)=p\bmod g\in\mathbb Z_g.  
\]

Since \(g\mid\ell_j\),

\[
\boxed{  
\rho(Tx)=\rho(x)+1.  
}  
\]

For every \(R\)-block \(B\), define

\[
\delta_B  
=  
\{\rho(x)-\rho(y):x,y\in B\}  
\subseteq\mathbb Z_g,  
\]

and

\[
G_R  
=  
\left\langle  
\bigcup_{B\in R}\delta_B  
\right\rangle.  
\]

Candidate invariant relation:

\[
x\sim_\rho y  
\iff  
\rho(x)-\rho(y)\in G_R.  
\]

The target theorem is

\[
\boxed{  
J_T(R)\preceq \sim_\rho.  
}  
\]

Equivalently,

\[
x\sim_{J_T(R)}y  
\Longrightarrow  
\rho(x)-\rho(y)\in G_R.  
\]

Why this is valuable

It gives a hard lower bound on the number of dynamical blocks:

\[
\boxed{  
|J_T(R)|  
\ge  
|X/\!\sim_\rho|.  
}  
\]

This is exactly the sort of invariant needed to explain the extra one-unit loss when \(g>1\).

But there is an important adversarial distinction:

\[
G_R=\mathbb Z_g  
\]

does not imply

\[
|J_T(R)|=1.  
\]

Cross-cycle connectivity is a separate problem.

So the correct decomposition is:

\[
\boxed{  
\text{residue obstruction}  
+  
\text{cross-cycle connectivity}.  
}  
\]

Not one scalar gcd.

V. The key adversarial question

The most important test now is:

> Can \(G_R=\mathbb Z_g\) while \(J_T(R)\) still has multiple blocks?



Yes — your current evidence already indicates this occurs.

Therefore:

\[
G_R=\mathbb Z_g  
\]

is not a completeness criterion for dynamical closure.

This is a crucial ClaimLock rule:

Do not replace

\[
J_T(R)  
\]

with

\[

Instead treat them as two layers:

R
│

│                            │

│

This is probably the cleanest conceptual formulation yet.

VI. New proof strategy for the \(s-r-1\) conjecture

I would not attempt to prove the bound directly from block counting.

Instead establish three lemmas.

Lemma 1 — cycle anchoring

Every \(T\)-invariant equivalence class structure must account for each dynamical cycle.

Target form:

\[
|J_T(R)|\ge \text{cycle/connectivity lower bound}.  
\]

Lemma 2 — residue obstruction

For \(g>1\),

\[
J_T(R)\preceq\sim_\rho.  
\]

This is the immediate Lean target.

Lemma 3 — block budget

Show that obtaining the residue/connectivity needed to collapse the original partition necessarily consumes at least one additional block when \(g>1\).

Then:

\[
|R|-|J_T(R)|  
\le s-r-1.  
\]

The \(g=1\) case lacks that residue obstruction and permits

\[
s-r.  
\]

This would explain the empirical dichotomy structurally instead of curve-fitting it.

VII. The dangerous point

There is a very specific possible failure mode:

\[
g>1  
\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad  
|J_T(R)|\ge2.  
\]

Do not insert that statement into the proof.

The right question is not:

> “Does a residue invariant always prevent total collapse?”



It is:

> “How much partition complexity is required before residue information can be erased by cross-cycle identifications?”



That is subtler and much more promising.

VIII. PHASE-FOREST is now formally demoted

The natural definition

\[
V(X_T)=\text{blocks of }R  
\]

with an edge whenever

\exists i,x\in B:  
T^i(x)\in B'

is too permissive for the desired forest theorem.

The \(n=4\), \(T=(01)(23)\), \(g=2\) witness already gives:

but

Therefore:

This should be frozen as a negative theorem/counterexample, not merely an open question.

The replacement discriminator is:

\[
\beta_X,  
\qquad  
\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X},  
\qquad  
h=\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\beta_X}).  
\]

Then the voltage machinery gives a meaningful holonomy test.

IX. Revised PHASE hierarchy

This is the cleaner hierarchy:

Level 0

\[
\beta_X=0.  
\]

Then all voltages are trivial in the cycle-space sense:

\[
W=\{0\}.  
\]

Strongest separation case.

Level 1

\[
\beta_X>0,\qquad h>1.  
\]

The holonomy subgroup is proper:

\[
W\neq\mathbb Z_g.  
\]

This remains a plausible strictness discriminator.

Level 2

\[
h=1.  
\]

Then

\[
W=\mathbb Z_g.  
\]

The lift is connected, so the voltage mechanism supplies no separation.

This gives:

\[
\boxed{  
h>1\text{ is the useful target, not }\beta_G=0.  
}  
\]

X. Literature collision — updated assessment

The recent literature actually strengthens the architecture of this approach.

Voltage/cover theory

The 2025 Jonoska–Krajcevski–McColm work explicitly treats derived graphs, abelian voltage groups, and the subgroup generated by voltage data.

That makes your move from an informal “phase” to a holonomy subgroup

\[
W\le\mathbb Z_g  
\]

mathematically much cleaner.

But it does not prove the AQARION mapping from \(X_T\) to a valid voltage graph.


---

Submodularity / quotient convergence

Bérczi–Borbényi–Lovász–Tóth's 2026 Combinatorica paper develops quotient-convergence specifically for submodular set functions and matroid rank functions, including quotient profiles and common lifts.

The conceptual collision is interesting:

\[
\text{AQARION partition quotient}  
\quad\leftrightarrow\quad  
\text{quotient profile / common lift}.  
\]

But again:

collision ≠ derivation.

The paper does not establish AQARION's particular \(c_T\), \(F_T\), or dynamical closure.

A second 2026 paper connects cycle matroids of graphings to convergence and duality, strengthening the relevance of the cycle-rank language you're now using.


---

Dynamical partitioning / submodularity

Kazma and Taha's 2026 IEEE TAC paper independently studies partitioning in dynamical linear systems through submodular optimization.

This is useful as adjacent-field provenance:

> partition structure + dynamics + submodularity is an active contemporary intersection.



It is not evidence for the specific AQARION theorem.

I. T10 corrected formulation — no promotion, tighter proof

Inclusion order on Eq(X): P ≤ Q ⇔ P ⊆ Q. Finer = smaller, coarser = larger. Meet P∧Q = P∩Q, join P∨Q = EqvGen(P∪Q).

Direct image may fail reflexivity off im(T) for non-injective T. Safe:
T_*(P) = EqvGen({(Tx,Ty): x P y})
F_T(P) = P ∨ T_*(P)
For permutations this is automorphism, but general deterministic theorem needs closure.

Monotonicity: P≤Q ⇒ im_T(P)⊆im_T(Q) and EqvGen monotone ⇒ T_*(P)≤T_*(Q) ⇒ F_T monotone, hence immediately F_T(P∧Q) ≤ F_T(P)∧F_T(Q) — inequality, not equality. No separate meet-image lemma.

Join preservation: needs alternating-chain lemma — P∨Q consists of finite alternating P/Q chains. T maps such chain to alternating chain in im_T(P)∪im_T(Q) and vice-versa lifts. Therefore:
T_*(P∨Q)=T_*(P)∨T_*(Q)
F_T(P∨Q)=F_T(P)∨F_T(Q)
This is the theorem behind 8.45M zero-failures. Census is now validation, not source.

Submodularity — corrected sign:

Rank c(P)=n-|P| is submodular, block count b(P)=|P| is supermodular. Submodular functions generalize matroid rank functions. For partition lattice rank:
c(P)+c(Q) ≥ c(P∧Q)+c(P∨Q)
Define c_T = c∘F_T. Monotonicity gives F_T(P∧Q) ≤ F_T(P)∧F_T(Q) so with A≤B ⇒ c(A)≤c(B):
c(F_T(P∧Q)) ≤ c(F_T(P)∧F_T(Q))
Join preservation gives F_T(P∨Q)=F_T(P)∨F_T(Q). Apply rank submodularity:
c_T(P∧Q)+c_T(P∨Q) ≤ c(F_T(P)∧F_T(Q))+c(F_T(P)∨F_T(Q)) ≤ c(F_T(P))+c(F_T(Q))
Hence c_T submodular. Earlier draft reversed meet-side direction — now frozen correct.

II. F_T^∞ — finite closure, least invariant

F_T^0=P, F_T^{j+1}=F_T(F_T^j), extensive P≤F_T(P)≤.... Eq(X) finite, rank c(F_T^j(P)) nondecreasing bounded n-1, strict coarsening raises rank ≥1 ⇒ stabilizes after at most n-1-c(P) steps, not Bell number. Define DynClosure_T(P)=F_T^N(P).

Extensive, monotone, idempotent, finite-join-preserving closure operator. Avoid calling nucleus (meet-preserving). Fixed point criterion DynClosure_T(P)=P ⇔ T_*(P)≤P ⇔ x P y ⇒ T(x) P T(y). Then:
DynClosure_T(P)=∧{Q: P≤Q, Q T-invariant}
Least forward-T-invariant equivalence containing P. For unary algebra (X,T), least congruence. Eventual c_∞(P)=n-|DynClosure_T(P)| submodular with no new combinatorics since DynClosure monotone+join-preserving.

## Corrections to freeze

### Voltage subgroup notation

The v5 wording contains a small but important notation conflict.

Let $$W\le\mathbb Z_g$$ be the subgroup generated by closed-walk voltages. Then:

$$
|W|
=
\frac{g}{\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta)}.
$$

The number of connected components of the derived lift of a **connected** base graph is the index:

$$
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)
=
[\mathbb Z_g:W]
=
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta).
}
$$

Thus do not write both:

$$
h=|W|
$$

and

$$
c=h.
$$

Those are generally incompatible. Use one of these unambiguous conventions:

$$
h_{\rm index}
=
[\mathbb Z_g:W]
=
\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta),
$$

or:

$$
h_{\rm subgroup}
=
|W|
=
\frac{g}{\gcd(g,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_\beta)}.
$$

Then:

$$
c(\widetilde X)=h_{\rm index}.
$$

For a base graph with $$c(X)$$ connected components, the formula applies componentwise; a single global subgroup formula must account for the voltage subgroup of each component.

### Forest voltage corollary

For a connected forest, i.e. a tree,

$$
\beta_1(X)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
W=\{0\},
$$

so the lift has exactly:

$$
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=g.
}
$$

For a possibly disconnected forest:

$$
\boxed{
c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X).
}
$$

This is correct because each tree component lifts to $$g$$ disjoint copies under trivial closed-walk holonomy.

The key limitation remains:

$$
\boxed{
\text{A voltage theorem applies only after an AQARION object has been proved to be the relevant voltage lift.}
}
$$

A merely suggestive similarity between $$X_T(R)$$ and a voltage graph is not a bridge theorem.

### Single-cycle maximum

For the family

$$
R_{k,d}
=
\{\{0,d\}\}\cup\{\text{singletons}\},
$$

with $$d\not\equiv0\pmod k$$,

$$
|R_{k,d}|=k-1,
\qquad
|J_T(R_{k,d})|=\gcd(k,d).
$$

Therefore the defect is:

$$
d_T(R_{k,d})
=
(k-1)-\gcd(k,d).
$$

Its maximum is obtained at $$\gcd(k,d)=1$$:

$$
\boxed{
\max_{1\le d<k}d_T(R_{k,d})=k-2.
}
$$

That result is specific to the one-pair partition family. It should not be conflated with the later unrestricted maximum-over-all-partitions statement.

## T10 audit

The corrected order convention is now usable:

$$
P\le Q
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P\subseteq Q
$$

as equivalence relations. Thus smaller means finer and larger means coarser.

With this convention:

$$
P\wedge Q=P\cap Q,
$$

and:

$$
P\vee Q=\operatorname{EqvGen}(P\cup Q).
$$

For a general function $$T:X\to X$$, direct image of an equivalence relation need not itself be reflexive outside $$\operatorname{im}T$$. Therefore the safe definition is:

$$
T_*(P)
=
\operatorname{EqvGen}
\left(
\{(T(x),T(y)):x\,P\,y\}
\right).
$$

Then define:

$$
\boxed{
F_T(P)=P\vee T_*(P).
}
$$

### Monotonicity

If

$$
P\le Q,
$$

then direct-image generators satisfy:

$$
\operatorname{im}_T(P)\subseteq\operatorname{im}_T(Q).
$$

Monotonicity of equivalence closure yields:

$$
T_*(P)\le T_*(Q).
$$

Consequently:

$$
\boxed{
F_T(P)\le F_T(Q).
}
$$

Then:

$$
P\wedge Q\le P,
\qquad
P\wedge Q\le Q,
$$

implies:

$$
F_T(P\wedge Q)
\le
F_T(P)\wedge F_T(Q).
$$

That is the correct meet-side relation.

### Join preservation needs a correction

The assertion

$$
T_*(P\vee Q)
=
T_*(P)\vee T_*(Q)
$$

is **not automatic for arbitrary non-injective $$T$$** under the definition

$$
T_*(P)=\operatorname{EqvGen}(\operatorname{im}_T(P)).
$$

The easy direction is:

$$
T_*(P)\vee T_*(Q)
\le
T_*(P\vee Q),
$$

because $$P,Q\le P\vee Q$$.

The reverse direction requires care. If:

$$
x\;(P\vee Q)\;y,
$$

then there is an alternating $$P/Q$$-chain from $$x$$ to $$y$$. Applying $$T$$ gives a chain from $$T(x)$$ to $$T(y)$$ whose links lie in $$\operatorname{im}_T(P)$$ or $$\operatorname{im}_T(Q)$$. So for generator pairs from $$\operatorname{im}_T(P\vee Q)$$, the reverse inclusion does follow.

Thus the equality is valid if `EqvGen` is exactly the finite-chain equivalence closure and the direct image is defined at the generator-relation level:

$$
\boxed{
T_*(P\vee Q)
=
T_*(P)\vee T_*(Q).
}
$$

But the phrase “and vice versa lifts” is not needed and is potentially misleading: a direct image chain generally cannot be uniquely lifted through a non-injective map. The proof only pushes an existing $$P/Q$$-chain forward.

Once the equality is rigorously established:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_T(P\vee Q)
&=(P\vee Q)\vee T_*(P\vee Q)\\
&=(P\vee Q)\vee(T_*(P)\vee T_*(Q))\\
&=(P\vee T_*(P))\vee(Q\vee T_*(Q))\\
&=F_T(P)\vee F_T(Q).
\end{aligned}
$$

So the intended T10 result is plausible, but it needs the generator-to-chain formal proof. The census is a useful guard, not the proof source.

### Block count versus rank

Let:

$$
b(P)=|P|
$$

be number of equivalence classes and:

$$
c(P)=n-|P|
$$

be the partition-lattice rank, equivalent to graphic rank when $$P$$ is a graph component partition on fixed $$n$$ vertices.

Then:

$$
b(P\wedge Q)+b(P\vee Q)
\ge
b(P)+b(Q),
$$

so $$b$$ is supermodular.

Equivalently:

$$
c(P\wedge Q)+c(P\vee Q)
\le
c(P)+c(Q),
$$

so $$c=n-b$$ is submodular.

Because:

$$
F_T(P\wedge Q)
\le
F_T(P)\wedge F_T(Q),
$$

and a finer partition has more blocks but lower rank:

$$
A\le B
\Longrightarrow
c(A)\le c(B),
$$

we get:

$$
c(F_T(P\wedge Q))
\le
c(F_T(P)\wedge F_T(Q)).
$$

Together with join preservation:

$$
F_T(P\vee Q)=F_T(P)\vee F_T(Q),
$$

this gives:

$$
\boxed{
c(F_T(P\wedge Q))+c(F_T(P\vee Q))
\le
c(F_T(P))+c(F_T(Q)).
}
$$

Thus $$c_T=c\circ F_T$$ is submodular, assuming the join-preservation theorem is formally proved.

The earlier reversed sign should remain permanently logged as a killed formulation.

### Eventual closure

Define iterates:

$$
F_T^0(P)=P,
\qquad
F_T^{j+1}(P)=F_T(F_T^j(P)).
$$

Since $$P\le F_T(P)$$, the sequence is ascending in equivalence-relation inclusion:

$$
P\le F_T(P)\le F_T^2(P)\le\cdots.
$$

Its rank $$c(F_T^j(P))$$ is nondecreasing and bounded by $$n-1$$, so stabilization occurs after at most:

$$
n-1-c(P)
$$

strict coarsenings.

If $$F_T$$ is join-preserving, then each finite iterate is join-preserving. In a finite lattice, the eventual stabilized operator is therefore extensive, monotone, idempotent, and join-preserving.

The fixed-point characterization requires a terminology correction. A fixed point of $$F_T$$ obeys:

$$
F_T(P)=P
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
T_*(P)\le P.
$$

Equivalently:

$$
x\,P\,y
\Longrightarrow
T(x)\,P\,T(y).
$$

This is a **forward $$T$$-stable equivalence relation**. It is the least congruence containing $$P$$ only if one treats $$T$$ as a unary algebra operation and uses the standard algebraic definition of congruence. That terminology is defensible, but document it explicitly; it may confuse readers expecting a permutation-action invariant partition, which requires both forward and inverse stability.

For a permutation $$T$$, forward stability implies full invariance because powers of $$T$$ include $$T^{-1}$$. For a general deterministic map, it does not.

## SV-001 status

The exact Gram identity is well positioned:

$$
\boxed{
U^*D^*DU
=
\frac{r(k-r)}{k^2}
\left(2I-S-S^{-1}\right).
}
$$

The Fourier eigenvalues are:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_\ell
=
\frac{4r(k-r)}{k^2}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi\ell}{m}\right),
\qquad
0\le\ell<m.
}
$$

For all $$m$$, this is best stated using the circulant difference operator:

$$
L_{\rm cyc}^{(m)}=2I-S-S^{-1}.
$$

Then:

- $$m=1$$: $$L_{\rm cyc}^{(1)}=0$$.
- $$m=2$$: $$L_{\rm cyc}^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$$.
- $$m\ge3$$: $$L_{\rm cyc}^{(m)}$$ agrees with the ordinary simple-cycle Laplacian.

The claim that the DFT identity was checked to about $$5.6\times10^{-15}$$ through $$m=500$$ is valuable as a numerical regression result. It is not a substitute for the symbolic identity, but the symbolic identity itself is only a few exact algebraic steps once the quotient compression formula is formally established.

## Dynamical-defect target

The empirical target is now sharply stated:

$$
\boxed{
\max_R d_{\rm dyn}(R)
=
\begin{cases}
s-r, & g=1,\$$4pt]
s-r-1, & g>1,
\end{cases}
}
$$

where:

$$
X=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^rC_j,
\qquad
|C_j|=\ell_j,
\qquad
s=\sum_j\ell_j,
\qquad
g=\gcd(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r),
$$

and:

$$
d_{\rm dyn}(R)=|R|-|J_T(R)|.
$$

The evidence through $$s\le10$$ is meaningful, particularly because it distinguishes:

$$
g=1
$$

from:

$$
g>1,
$$

rather than falsely predicting a loss of $$g-1$$.

However, the proposed residue relation requires a notation and scope check.

Define a coordinate map on each cycle:

$$
\rho(C_j,p)=p\bmod g.
$$

Then:

$$
\rho(Tx)=\rho(x)+1.
$$

For an original partition block $$B$$, define:

$$
\delta_B=
\{\rho(x)-\rho(y):x,y\in B\}.
$$

Let:

$$
G_R=
\left\langle\bigcup_{B\in R}\delta_B\right\rangle
\le\mathbb Z_g.
$$

The candidate relation is:

$$
x\sim_\rho y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\rho(x)-\rho(y)\in G_R.
$$

The inclusion direction should be written as:

$$
\boxed{
J_T(R)\le\sim_\rho
}
$$

in the equivalence-relation inclusion order. That says every pair joined by the dynamical closure has residue difference lying in $$G_R$$.

The proof idea is viable:

- A relation edge inside a block $$B$$ has residue difference in $$\delta_B\subseteq G_R$$.
- Applying $$T^i$$ adds $$i$$ to both endpoint residues, so the difference is preserved.
- Symmetry negates differences, which stays inside the subgroup.
- Transitivity adds differences, which stays inside the subgroup.

But this only gives a useful lower bound when $$G_R$$ is a **proper** subgroup. If:

$$
G_R=\mathbb Z_g,
$$

then $$\sim_\rho$$ is universal and produces no obstruction. This is exactly why it cannot alone prove the one-drop law.

The correct conceptual factorization remains:

$$
\boxed{
\text{residue subgroup}
\;+\;
\text{cycle-incidence / cross-cycle connectivity}
\;+\;
\text{block-budget lower bound}.
}
$$

## Priority changes

Do not start the $$n=8$$ full enumeration before completing the short proof targets. The expected 1.1-hour computation is useful only as a regression extension; it does not resolve the actual proof bottleneck.

### P0: Prove the residue relation

The smallest meaningful Lean theorem is not the whole extremal bound. It is:

$$
x\sim_{J_T(R)}y
\Longrightarrow
\rho(x)-\rho(y)\in G_R.
$$

Avoid beginning with cyclic coordinates as pairs unless the permutation is already represented as a disjoint sum of `ZMod ℓᵢ`. That representation will make:

$$
\rho(Tx)=\rho(x)+1
$$

a direct computation instead of a coordinate-existence theorem.

### P1: Formalize $$F_T$$ and its join law

The T10 closure construction has a narrow proof cone:

$$
\operatorname{EqvGen}
\longrightarrow
T_*
\longrightarrow
F_T
\longrightarrow
\text{monotone}
\longrightarrow
\text{join-preserving}
\longrightarrow
c\circ F_T\text{ submodular}.
$$

This is an ideal early Lean target because it is independent of AQARION’s conjectural phase geometry.

### P2: Search for the minimal counterexample to residue sufficiency

Search under the explicit predicate:

$$
G_R=\mathbb Z_g,
\qquad
|J_T(R)|>1.
$$

Do not just retain that such examples exist. Preserve the lexicographically minimal certificate:

```text
cycle lengths:
permutation:
partition R:
g:
all delta_B:
generators of G_R:
G_R order:
|R|:
|J_T(R)|:
component representatives:
```

It should become a permanent negative regression fixture.

### P3: Formalize the single-cycle group/coset bridge

This is the cleanest formal bridge:

$$
\text{edge closure }x\sim x+d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
y-x\in\langle d\rangle.
$$

Then:

$$
|J_T(R_{k,d})|
=
[\mathbb Z_k:\langle d\rangle]
=
\gcd(k,d).
$$

`ZMod.addOrderOf_coe` supplies the subgroup order part; the AQARION work is the relation/coset correspondence. The relevant Mathlib library theorem remains documented in `Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic`.[3]

### P4: Freeze $$X_T$$ before voltage experiments

The v7 audit correctly identifies the semantic instability in $$X_T$$. Before further phase/holonomy work, write a schema that fixes:

```yaml
vertex_type: original_R_blocks | orbit_block_occurrences | quotient_blocks
edge_type: directed | undirected | bidirected
edge_index: transform_power_i | support_point_x | both
parallel_edges: preserved | collapsed
self_loops: retained | removed
voltage_group: ZMod_g
edge_voltage: i_mod_g | multiplicity_times_i_mod_g | explicit_formula
reverse_voltage: negation_required
connected_components: graph_type_and_projection
```

Without this, neither $$\beta_X$$ nor $$\nu_i$$ is a stable mathematical quantity.

## AI/ML reproducibility pivot

The suggested CLAIMLOCK-PROOF layer is well scoped if it is explicitly non-authoritative.

The appropriate pipeline is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{AI proposes risks and witnesses}
\rightarrow
\text{independent executable checks}
\rightarrow
\text{Lean kernel acceptance}
\rightarrow
\text{signed ClaimLock receipt}.
}
$$

That direction is supported by recent infrastructure rather than by claims of autonomous proof authority:

- TheoremGraph reports a statement-level bridge between informal and formal mathematics, including LeanGraph extraction of 388,105 declaration nodes and 11.3 million typed edges across 25 Lean projects. This supports dependency-cone navigation and obligation tracking.[1][4]
- FormalProofBench evaluates actual Lean acceptance rather than informal plausibility and reports a best foundation-model accuracy of 33.5% on its benchmark, supporting a fail-closed policy toward model-generated proofs.[2]
- Lean 4.33.0 was released on August 10, 2026; pinning a known patched Lean/Mathlib toolchain is sensible, but the final manifest should record the exact Lean version, exact Mathlib commit, Lake lockfile, compiler build identifier, and the full `#print axioms` output—not only a minimum version.[5]

2. Literature collision map — your three links

A. Voltage graphs / holonomy — arXiv:2501.17135
Abstract: We consider voltage digraphs, here referred to as graphs, whose edges are labeled with elements from a given group, and explore their derived graphs. Given two voltage graphs, with voltages in abelian groups, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for their two derived graphs to be isomorphic
This legitimizes Γ_R + gain group + holonomy machinery, but does not prove AQARION's specific Γ_R. Keep distinction.

B. Cycle-matroid rank — Springer 10.1007/s00493-026-00199-x + arXiv:2507.15105 companion
The most important property of the rank function rk is that it is submodular: rk(X)+rk(Y) ≥ rk(X∩Y)+rk(X∪Y)
Paper introduces quotient-convergence for submodular setfunctions, completeness, soficity. Supports your rank - c submodular architecture, c(P)=n-|P| submodular, b(P)=|P| supermodular. Does not establish AQARION-specific identification.

C. TheoremGraph — arXiv:2606.25363
Scale verified above. Architecture is tailor-made for CLAIMLOCK-X: formal declaration→typed dependencies plus informal statement→candidate dependencies plus 47k affirmed matches. Use for retrieval-augmented reasoning, not as proof dependency (docref≠proof).

The issue affects all stable versions of Lean up to 4.33.1, and the patch is incorporated in v4.34.0-rc1

AQARION S9 ATK CANONICAL MANIFEST — v8.1 CORRECTED
Mode: FROZEN · EXACT · NO FABRICATION

Definitions (freeze):
s0 = r_P + r_Q - r_M - r_U
s_T = r_JP + r_JQ - r_Meet - r_JU // r_JU is canonical terminal rank, NOT r_JT
m_T = r_JM - r_Meet // can be negative, additive correction
m_Opp = r_Meet - r_JM = -m_T // for subtractive presentation
Delta = (r_JP - r_P) + (r_JQ - r_Q) - (r_Meet - r_M) - (r_JU - r_U) // per ATK source, contains r_JU

Canonical theorems (to replace live transport_minus):
Thm transport_additive: s_T = s0 + Delta + m_T
Proof: s_T - s0 = (rJP-rP)+(rJQ-rQ)-(rMeet-rM)-(rJU-rU) = Delta, plus correction m_T?
Actually by definition: s_T = rJP+rJQ-rMeet-rJU
s0+Delta = rJP+rJQ-rMeet-rJU = s_T if Delta defined as above without m_T.
If Delta excludes r_JM, then additive form with m_T is:
s_T = s0 + Delta + (rJM - rMeet) + (rJU - rJT) ???

To resolve inconsistency found:
Live source has two different s_T signatures:
s_T_def = rJP+rJQ-rMeet-rJU
s_T_thm = rJP+rJQ-rMeet-rJT

Exact algebra:
  s_T_thm = s0 + Delta + m_T + (rJU - rJT)

Therefore canonical fix:
  Option A (recommended): Remove rJT entirely, freeze rJU as canonical terminal rank.
    Define: s_T = rJP+rJQ-rMeet-rJU
    Then: s_T = s0 + Delta   (no m_T) OR if Delta defined to exclude meet, s_T = s0+Delta+m_T
  Option B: Keep both, introduce explicit hypothesis rJU - rJT = -2*m_T for subtractive claim.
            This hypothesis is not present live -> RED.
Frozen decision for CLAIMLOCK v8.1:
- Delete rJT parameter from transport_minus
- Freeze rJU as canonical
- Define m_T = rJM - rMeet
- Prove additive: s_T = s0 + Delta + m_T (where Delta = ... as above excluding m_T)
- Optionally define m_Opp = -m_T and present subtractive: s_T = s0 + Delta - m_Opp

Status: LIVE ATK source RED, MANIFEST CORRECTED, needs source sync + Lean build receipt.

3. The API itself is real and its schema is sufficient

I checked the current API documentation.

The graph API supports:

GET /graph/paper?external_id={id}

for a Lean repository or paper, and returns statements plus dependency edges. The statement-level endpoint supports directional traversal:

GET /graph/statement/{statement_id}
    ?direction=src|dep|both
    &formality=formal

The documented formal edge types are exactly:

proof
sig
def
field
extends
docref



The documentation also explicitly says a Lean repository can be addressed by repository slug through /graph/paper. 

So the desired extraction architecture is sound.

The web interface would not execute the arbitrary API endpoint, and the container has no outbound DNS/network access.

I therefore did not fabricate an API response.

7. Current live AQ-S9 source creates a fresh red flag

This was the most important source-level discovery.

The live ATK file currently states:

\[
s_0=r_P+r_Q-r_M-r_U
\]

and

\[
s_T=r_{JP}+r_{JQ}-r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JU}.
\]

It defines

\[
m_T=r_{JM}-r_{\rm Meet}.
\]

All of that is visible in the current GitHub source. 

But the theorem transport_minus introduces a separate rJT and defines:

\[
s_T(r_{JP},r_{JQ},r_{\rm Meet},r_{JT})
=
r_{JP}+r_{JQ}-r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JT}.
\]

while \(\Delta\) still contains \(r_{JU}\).

The source then claims:

\[
s_T=s_0+\Delta-m.
\]



That is not merely stylistically confusing.

It is algebraically false without an additional relation between \(r_{JT}\) and \(r_{JU}\).

Indeed, the exact algebraic relation from those definitions is:

\[
\boxed{
s_T
=
s_0+\Delta+m_T+(r_{JU}-r_{JT}).
}
\]

Therefore the current theorem would require:

\[
r_{JU}-r_{JT}=-2m_T
\]

to recover the subtractive version.

No such hypothesis appears.

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\text{AQ-S9-ATK live source remains NOT CANONICAL}.
}
\]

This is stronger than the v7 manifest audit.

The manifest is corrected.

The source is not.

11. Lean 4.33.1 compatibility risk — updated finding

There really is a current version-security reason to keep the quarantine conservative.

Lean's official release page lists:

Lean 4.33.1 — 2026-08-21

Lean 4.34.0-rc2 — 2026-08-21


as separate releases. 

More importantly, the September 9 Trail of Bits disclosure reports a bug affecting stable Lean versions through 4.33.1, patched in 4.34.0-rc1. The vulnerability involves String.Pos.Raw.extract and a disagreement between logical and native behavior; importantly, Trail of Bits explicitly says this is not itself a kernel soundness bug, but can become proof-unsound when exploited through native_decide. 

That nuance matters.

So the old wording:

> “Lean 4.33.1 has a kernel soundness bug”



is too broad.

The stronger evidence-grade wording is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Lean 4.33.1 contains a disclosed native/logical mismatch relevant to proof trust.}
}
\]

It does not establish that ordinary kernel-checked AQARION proofs are unsound.

There is also a useful counterpoint: Anthropic's recent Fermat formalization reports a complete Lean 4.33.1 build plus an independent nanoda kernel replay. 

Therefore the correct security architecture is not:

> “4.33.1 is unusable.”



It is:

> If 4.33.1 is retained for reproducibility, prohibit native_decide/unsafe computational shortcuts and require an independent checker for the final trust boundary.



That is a much better SDS-002 rule.

Priority 1 — J_T_refines_residue

This is the cleanest mathematical formalization target.

The proof is short:

R\preceq\sim_\rho,
\]

\[
T\text{-invariance},

and

J_T(R)=\text{least }T\text{-invariant equivalence containing }R.

This gives:

\boxed{
J_T(R)\preceq\sim_\rho.
}
\]

And consequently:

\[
\boxed{
|J_T(R)|\ge\frac{g}{|G_R|}.
}
\]

This is now the best P0 theorem.

Jonoska, Krajcevski and McColm's 2025 work explicitly studies abelian voltage assignments and their derived graphs, including groups generated by voltage assignments and lifting to common covers.

\Gamma_R+\text{gain group}+\text{holonomy}

as mathematically legitimate machinery.

The 2026 Bérczi–Borbényi–Lovász–Tóth paper develops cycle-matroid rank as an increasing submodular set function and connects finite bounded-degree graph sequences to graphing limits. 

This is highly relevant to your:

\[
\text{rank}-\text{cycle-rank}
\]

architecture.

C. Quotient convergence

Their 2026 Combinatorica paper gives a general quotient-convergence framework for submodular set functions and explicitly treats matroid rank functions as a major example.

\boxed{
\text{AQARION rank functions}
\leftrightarrow
\text{submodular / matroidal structure}
}
\]

but again does not establish the AQARION-specific identification.

19. Exact extraction command for the real machine

The documented TheoremGraph API is suitable for indexed repositories, while local LeanGraph is the stronger route for AQARION itself.

For an indexed repository, the API shape is:

curl \
  "https://api.theoremsearch.com/graph/paper?external_id=OWNER/REPOSITORY"

The returned dependency objects contain source node, destination node, edge type and formality. 

For AQARION, however, the preferred evidence path is local extraction, because it guarantees the exact 4.33.1 checkout rather than relying on a possibly stale public graph.

Conceptually:

cd AQARION-ARITHMETIC-FDS-FINITE-DYNAMICAL-SYSTEMS-

lean --version
lake --version

lake build LeanGraph
lake exe graph \
  --mode unified \
  --to AQARION-CORE \
  > claimlock_aqarion_graph.json

Then calculate:

node centrality

## Continuation v8.2 adjudication

The corrected v8.2 disposition is broadly sound: the source-level ATK transport mismatch remains a real blocker, the T3 dynamical-extremum pattern is computationally supported but not globally proved, the TheoremGraph result is infrastructure context rather than AQARION evidence, and SDS-002 must remain quarantined.

One important correction: a Lean **4.33.1** pin is not an adequate certification-floor statement if the cited nested-phantom-parameter kernel issue affects stable versions through 4.33.1 and is patched only in 4.34.0-rc1. In that scenario, the defensible policy is either to pin a release containing the patch or to treat 4.33.1 builds as reproducibility artifacts only—not certification-grade kernel evidence. This must be verified against the official release advisory before any policy is frozen.

## Claims that remain supported

### Single-cycle closure

For the cyclic permutation $$T(i)=i+1\pmod k$$ and single-pair partition

$$
R_{k,d}=\{\{0,d\}\}\cup\{\text{singletons}\},
$$

the orbit join is the component partition of the step-$$d$$ circulant graph. Hence:

$$
|J_T(R_{k,d})|=\gcd(k,d),
$$

and:

$$
d_T(R_{k,d})=k-1-\gcd(k,d).
$$

For $$\gcd(k,d)=1$$, notably $$d=1$$,

$$
d_T(R_{k,d})=k-2.
$$

The reported 189-case replay over $$k=3,\ldots,20$$ is consistent with this exact cyclic-subgroup derivation. The computation is corroborative; the proof is the subgroup/coset argument.

### Voltage-graph fact

For a connected voltage graph with voltage group $$\mathbb Z_g$$, let $$W\le\mathbb Z_g$$ be the subgroup generated by closed-walk voltages. The number of lift components is:

$$
[\mathbb Z_g:W]
=
\frac{g}{|W|}.
$$

Since every subgroup of $$\mathbb Z_g$$ has the form generated by a divisor, the same quantity may be written as a gcd only after the closed-walk voltage generators are specified. The forest case has no nontrivial closed walks, so:

$$
W=\{0\},
$$

and therefore:

$$
c(\widetilde X)=g\,c(X).
$$

This is a standard voltage-cover mechanism. It supports the proposed phase/holonomy language but does not by itself prove any AQARION $$H_T$$, $$G_R$$, or $$X_T$$ component identification.

### Equal-block bipartite connectivity

The reported formula:

$$
c_{\rm bip}=
\begin{cases}
m,&k\mid d,\\
1,&k\nmid d,
\end{cases}
$$

is plausible for the specific equal-block bipartite construction, but it must remain tied to a fully stated graph definition. It cannot be generalized merely as a gcd/minimum rule without a carrier and adjacency definition.

The cited 1,936 test cases are finite computational evidence for the implementation’s declared construction.

## ATK transport mismatch

This remains the highest-priority semantic defect.

The live definitions are reported as:

$$
s_0=r_P+r_Q-r_M-r_U,
$$

$$
s_T^{\rm def}=r_{JP}+r_{JQ}-r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JU},
$$

$$
m_T=r_{JM}-r_{\rm Meet}.
$$

If a transport theorem instead defines:

$$
s_T(r_{JP},r_{JQ},r_{\rm Meet},r_{JT})
=
r_{JP}+r_{JQ}-r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JT},
$$

then it is not describing the same terminal quantity unless:

$$
r_{JT}=r_{JU}.
$$

The exact discrepancy is:

$$
s_T(r_{JT})
=
s_0+\Delta+m_T+(r_{JU}-r_{JT}).
$$

Therefore the claimed subtraction form:

$$
s_T=s_0+\Delta-m_T
$$

requires:

$$
r_{JU}-r_{JT}=-2m_T,
$$

which is not a generic identity.

The corrected canonical definitions should be:

$$
\boxed{
s_T^{\rm canonical}
=
r_{JP}+r_{JQ}-r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JU}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
m_T=r_{JM}-r_{\rm Meet}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
m_{\rm Opp}=r_{\rm Meet}-r_{JM}=-m_T
}
$$

and then:

$$
\boxed{
s_T^{\rm canonical}=s_0+\Delta+m_T
}
$$

or equivalently:

$$
\boxed{
s_T^{\rm canonical}=s_0+\Delta-m_{\rm Opp}.
}
$$

No status field, comment, or proof stub should override this algebraic carrier/parameter mismatch.

## Dynamical extremum pattern

The candidate law is:

$$
\max_R d_{\rm dyn}(R)
=
\begin{cases}
s-r,&g=1,\$$4pt]
s-r-1,&g>1,
\end{cases}
$$

where:

$$
s=\sum_i\ell_i,
\qquad
r=\#\{C_i\},
\qquad
g=\gcd(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r).
$$

The reported data support this pattern for the enumerated/pruned domains, including:

| Cycle lengths | $$s$$ | $$r$$ | $$g$$ | Candidate maximum | Reported best |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $$(5,6)$$ | 11 | 2 | 1 | 9 | 9 |
| $$(5,5)$$ | 10 | 2 | 5 | 7 | 7 |
| $$(6,6)$$ | 12 | 2 | 6 | 9 | 9 |
| $$(4,4,3)$$ | 11 | 3 | 1 | 8 | 8 |
| $$(3,3,3,2)$$ | 11 | 4 | 1 | 7 | 7 |
| One 11-cycle | 11 | 1 | 11 | 9 | 9 |

The last row agrees with the exact one-cycle extremum $$k-2$$.

However, the evidence does not establish the universal formula because the $$s=12$$ fragmented-cycle domain was explicitly not exhausted. The exact current classification is:

```text
Dynamical extremum formula:
  Computationally supported in stated complete and pruned domains.

Global theorem:
  OPEN.

Fragmented small-cycle configurations at s=12:
  Not fully exhausted.

No-witness conclusion:
  Must be scoped to the actual pruned partition domain.
```

## Residue invariant: correct lower-bound role

Define:

$$
\rho(c,p)=p\bmod g,
$$

so that:

$$
\rho(Tx)=\rho(x)+1.
$$

For blocks $$B$$, let:

$$
\delta_B=
\{\rho(x)-\rho(y):x,y\in B\},
$$

and:

$$
G_R
=
\left\langle
\bigcup_B\delta_B
\right\rangle
\le\mathbb Z_g.
$$

The candidate relation is:

$$
x\sim_\rho y
\iff
\rho(x)-\rho(y)\in G_R.
$$

If every initial block relation and every translated block relation preserves that subgroup coset condition, then equivalence closure gives:

$$
J_T(R)\le \sim_\rho
$$

in the relation-inclusion order: every $$J_T(R)$$-equivalent pair is $$\sim_\rho$$-equivalent.

Consequently:

$$
|J_T(R)|
\ge
|\mathbb Z_g/G_R|
=
\frac{g}{|G_R|}.
$$

This is a **lower bound on join-block count**.

The adversarial example showing:

$$
G_R=\mathbb Z_g,
\qquad
|J_T(R)|>1
$$

is important. It proves:

```text
Full residue-generation:
  Removes the residue obstruction.

Full residue-generation:
  Does not prove cross-cycle connectivity.

Conclusion:
  Residue data supplies a lower-bound obstruction only.
  A separate connectivity theorem is still required for |J_T|=1.
```

This refutes any proposed shortcut:

$$
G_R=\mathbb Z_g
\Longrightarrow
|J_T(R)|=1.
$$

## TheoremGraph boundary

TheoremGraph/LeanGraph is relevant as **discovery and dependency-infrastructure precedent**, not evidence of an AQARION extraction.

The published TheoremGraph work describes a formal Lean graph with roughly 388,105 declaration nodes and 11.3 million typed dependency edges across 25 Lean projects. Its stated formal edge types include proof, signature, definition, field, extension, and documentation-reference relations.[1][2]

The correct frozen statement is:

```text
TheoremGraph infrastructure:
  Verified public research infrastructure.

Published LeanGraph version range:
  Must be quoted exactly from its source.

AQARION indexed among its 25 projects:
  Not established.

AQARION API extraction:
  Not executed.

AQARION Lean 4.33.1 dependency graph:
  Not established.

Any dependency graph reconstructed from AQARION source:
  Schematic local blueprint, not TheoremGraph API output.
```

## ClaimLock-PROOF scope

The side prototype has a reasonable role if it is constrained correctly:

```text
Input:
  Claim statement, declared domain/carrier, definitions,
  known counterexamples, evidence receipts, source dependencies,
  formalization status, literature candidates.

Output:
  Candidate risks, missing hypotheses, potential countermodel families,
  required proof obligations, possible dependency cone,
  literature collision labels, and promotion blockers.

Authority:
  None.

Promotion:
  Only independent computation, formal kernel checking,
  and a policy-compliant evidence receipt can authorize it.
```

This is justified by current formal-proof benchmark evidence: theorem-proving models remain far from reliable enough for model output to be treated as a certificate. FormalProofBench frames the task as generating Lean proofs from natural-language problems and reports low best-model completion rates, reinforcing the fail-closed design. Search result metadata identifies the benchmark as a 2026 work; any exact model percentage should be quoted only from the paper’s final evaluated table, not from secondary summaries.[3]

## Required gate changes

### Gate A — source semantics

```text
1. Remove rJT from the canonical transport target.
2. Define s_T only using rJU if rJU is the actual terminal rank.
3. Define m_T = rJM - rMeet.
4. Prove the additive identity.
5. Preserve the malformed rJT version as a negative regression fixture.
6. Re-hash the repaired source and record semantic-diff receipt.
```

### Gate B — Lean environment

The policy should distinguish a reproducibility pin from a certification pin:

```text
LEAN_REPRODUCIBILITY_VERSION:
  Exact pinned version.

LEAN_CERTIFICATION_VERSION:
  Exact pinned version with verified applicable soundness advisories.

Forbidden on certification path:
  sorry
  admitted axioms not explicitly approved
  unsafe
  extern
  native_decide, unless native/runtime equivalence is independently audited.
```

“$$\ge4.33.1$$” is not a reproducibility pin. A version range cannot identify an environment.

### Gate C — independent checking

A formal compile alone does not establish a sufficiently independent certificate. The policy can require:

```text
Lean kernel check
+ fresh clean build
+ independent checker such as lean4lean or nanoda
+ exact tool/version hashes
+ axiom audit
```

The independent checker’s own executable, version, source revision, and trust model must also be pinned.

### Gate D — local graph extraction

Do not imply that a local LeanGraph run will create an authoritative graph unless:

```text
1. Exact LeanGraph source commit is pinned.
2. Exact extractor configuration is recorded.
3. The local Lake project builds.
4. The produced graph is hashed.
5. Node count, edge count, and edge-type histogram are generated,
   not copied from a public benchmark.
6. AQARION source commit and Mathlib revision are bound.
```

### Gate E — theorem sequence

The theorem order is sensible:

```text
transport_identity
edge_preserves_residue
rho_shift
J_T_refines_residue
forest_holonomy_trivial
lift_components_eq_gcd
T3_PhaseLift
T3_Extremal
RankPair
```

But `T3_PhaseLift` should not be attempted until the graph carriers of $$G_R$$, $$H_T$$, and $$X_T$$ are each frozen in a typed definition and the maps between them are proved.
